articles.title: Slippage and Spread: Why Your Fill Differs from the Quote
articles.summary: The price shown on a screen is usually the last trade or a mid-point. Actually trading crosses the spread — the gap between the highest standing bid and the lowest standing offer — so the executed price sits a little worse than the quote even in a calm market.

articles.title: Deepfaked Endorsements: When the Famous Face Is Not Real
articles.summary: AI tools can now produce convincing video and audio of well-known people saying things they never said. Scammers use this to fabricate interviews and live streams in which a famous founder or celebrity appears to promote a giveaway or a trading platform.

articles.title: A QR Code Is Just a Link You Can't Read
articles.summary: A QR code is a link or an address printed as a pattern — and unlike text, you cannot read it before opening it. Scammers exploit that by pasting their own stickers over legitimate codes on posters and terminals, or by circulating codes that encode their wallet address instead of the intended one.

articles.title: What Hash Rate Tells You About a Proof-of-Work Network
articles.summary: Hash rate measures how much computing power is being spent every second trying to produce the next block on a proof-of-work network such as Bitcoin. It is usually quoted in enormous units — today's networks are measured in exahashes, a billion billion attempts per second.

articles.title: Market Orders vs Limit Orders, in Plain Terms
articles.summary: Exchanges generally offer two basic ways to trade. A market order executes immediately at the best prices currently available. A limit order instead states a price, and waits: it only fills at that price or better, and may not fill at all.

articles.title: Browser Extensions Can Read What Your Wallet Sees
articles.summary: A browser extension with broad permissions can read and change what you see on the pages you visit. A malicious one can swap the destination address on a transfer page, alter a payment request, or capture what you type into a web wallet.

articles.title: A New Memecoin Fell Roughly 98% on Its First Day — a Reminder of How the Category Works
articles.summary: A widely publicised new memecoin lost close to 98% of its value within its first day of trading, according to reporting on 9–10 September 2026. The episode is a useful illustration of how the memecoin category behaves.

articles.title: Why Quantum Computing Keeps Coming Up in Bitcoin and Ethereum Debates
articles.summary: New quantum-computing hardware announcements have again put a long-running question back in front of crypto communities: could a future quantum computer break the cryptography that secures Bitcoin and Ethereum? The topic resurfaced around 9 September 2026 alongside fresh hardware news.

articles.title: Consensys Plans to Spin MetaMask Into Its Own Company
articles.summary: Consensys said it intends to separate MetaMask — one of the most widely used self-custody wallets — into its own standalone company, according to reporting on 9 September 2026.

articles.title: Your Recovery Phrase Is the Wallet
articles.summary: A recovery phrase — also called a seed phrase — is a list of words that can regenerate a crypto wallet and everything in it. Whoever holds the phrase controls the funds.

articles.title: Long-Con “Investment” Scams (Pig Butchering)
articles.summary: In these schemes a stranger builds a friendship or romance over weeks, then gradually introduces a “can't-miss” crypto opportunity on a platform they recommend.

articles.title: Why the Same Coin Shows Different Prices
articles.summary: Crypto trades on many venues at once, each with its own buyers and sellers, so the exact price can differ slightly from place to place at any instant.

articles.title: Security Note: Fake Hardware-Wallet Alerts Are Circulating
articles.summary: Two hardware-wallet makers, Trezor and BitBox, have warned users about fake “security alert” messages that impersonate the companies and try to rush people into urgent action. The warnings were reported on 9–10 September 2026.

articles.title: US Authorities Freeze About $52 Million Tied to a Crypto Scam Marketplace
articles.summary: US authorities moved against an online marketplace accused of underpinning global scams, restraining roughly $52 million in cryptocurrency linked to it, according to reporting on 9–10 September 2026.

articles.title: Fake Airdrops and Dangerous Token Approvals
articles.summary: Scam “airdrops” drop unfamiliar tokens into your wallet or advertise a claim site. Interacting can prompt you to approve a contract that then drains your assets.

articles.title: “Support” That Messages You First Is a Scam
articles.summary: A common trick is an impostor posing as customer support who reaches out first — in a DM, a reply, or a chat group — offering to “help” with a problem you mentioned.

articles.title: What “Market Cap” Means for a Crypto
articles.summary: A crypto's market capitalisation is its current price multiplied by the number of coins in circulation. It is a rough measure of the asset's total size, and it is why a low per-coin price does not by itself mean a coin is “cheap”.

articles.title: What a Transaction Hash (TXID) Is
articles.summary: Every confirmed transaction gets a unique identifier called a transaction hash, or TXID — a long string that acts as its receipt.

articles.title: What a Blockchain Actually Is
articles.summary: A blockchain is a shared ledger copied across many computers, where new entries are grouped into blocks and linked in order. Once recorded and confirmed, entries are extremely hard to alter.

articles.title: Hot Wallets vs Cold Wallets
articles.summary: A hot wallet is connected to the internet — an app or browser extension — making it convenient for frequent use but more exposed to online threats.

articles.title: How the Crypto Fear & Greed Index Works
articles.summary: The Fear & Greed Index compresses several market inputs — volatility, momentum, volume and more — into a single number from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed).

articles.title: What Happens When a Stablecoin “Depegs”
articles.summary: A stablecoin is meant to track a reference value, usually one dollar. A “depeg” is when its market price drifts away from that target.

articles.title: What “Gas” and Network Fees Are
articles.summary: Most blockchains charge a fee to process a transaction. On Ethereum and similar networks this is called “gas”, and it pays the network for the computation and space a transaction uses.

articles.title: What “Liquidity” Means in a Market
articles.summary: Liquidity is how easily an asset can be bought or sold without moving its price much. A liquid market has many buyers and sellers close together in price.

articles.title: Beware “Recovery” Scams After a Loss
articles.summary: People who have already lost crypto are targeted a second time by “recovery experts” who promise, for an up-front fee, to trace and return the stolen funds.

articles.title: What an All-Time High (ATH) Is
articles.summary: An all-time high is the highest price an asset has ever reached. You will also see all-time low (ATL) for the opposite.

articles.title: What Fully Diluted Valuation (FDV) Is
articles.summary: Fully diluted valuation estimates what a coin's market cap would be if every coin that will ever exist were already in circulation — price multiplied by the maximum or total supply.

articles.title: Coin vs Token — the Difference
articles.summary: A coin is the native asset of its own blockchain — Bitcoin on the Bitcoin network, Ether on Ethereum. It is used to pay that network's fees and secure it.

articles.title: What “Total Value Locked” (TVL) Means
articles.summary: Total value locked is the amount of assets currently deposited in a DeFi protocol — a rough gauge of how much people are using and trusting it.

articles.title: No One Legitimate Ever Needs Your Seed Phrase
articles.summary: The most direct crypto theft is simply getting you to reveal your recovery (seed) phrase. Once someone has it, they can recreate your wallet and move everything.

articles.title: What an NFT Is
articles.summary: An NFT, or non-fungible token, is a unique token that represents ownership of a specific item — art, a collectible, or access to something — recorded on a blockchain.

articles.title: What “Altcoin” Means
articles.summary: “Altcoin” is shorthand for any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin. The term covers everything from large, established networks to tiny, obscure tokens.

articles.title: What a “Layer 2” Is
articles.summary: A Layer 2 is a network built on top of a base blockchain (the Layer 1) to handle transactions more cheaply and quickly, then settle back to the main chain.

articles.title: A Simple “Verify Before You Trust” Checklist
articles.summary: Most crypto scams collapse against a few habits. Slow down when something feels urgent — pressure and countdowns are tools used to stop you thinking.

articles.title: Candlestick vs Line Charts
articles.summary: A line chart connects closing prices into a single line — clean and good for seeing the overall trend at a glance.

articles.title: What a Block Explorer Is
articles.summary: A block explorer is a website that lets anyone look up the public data on a blockchain — transactions, addresses, blocks and balances.

articles.title: What Bitcoin's “Halving” Means
articles.summary: Roughly every four years, the reward paid to Bitcoin miners for adding a block is cut in half. This is the halving, and it is written into Bitcoin's rules.

articles.title: Fake Job and “Task” Scams
articles.summary: These start as an easy remote job — rating apps, “boosting” listings, completing tasks — that pays small amounts at first, then asks you to deposit crypto to unlock higher earnings.

articles.title: What “DeFi” Means
articles.summary: DeFi, or decentralised finance, refers to financial services — trading, lending, borrowing — built from smart contracts rather than run by a company.

articles.title: When Returns Sound Too Good, They Usually Are
articles.summary: Fraudulent schemes often advertise steady, unusually high payouts that never seem to have a losing period — a pattern real markets do not produce.

articles.title: What a Whitepaper Is
articles.summary: A whitepaper is the document a crypto project publishes to explain what it does, how it works, and why it exists.

articles.title: The “Send 1, Get 2 Back” Giveaway Scam
articles.summary: A persistent scam promises that if you send some crypto to an address, you will get back double — often dressed up with a famous name, a countdown, and fake “proof” of others being paid.

articles.title: Clipboard-Hijacking Malware
articles.summary: Some malware silently watches your clipboard and, when it sees a crypto address, swaps in the attacker's address at the moment you paste.

articles.title: SIM-Swap Attacks and Why SMS Codes Are Weak
articles.summary: In a SIM-swap, an attacker convinces your mobile carrier to move your number to their device, then uses SMS codes to reset accounts and bypass text-based two-factor login.

articles.title: Proof of Work vs Proof of Stake
articles.summary: Both are ways a decentralised network agrees on which transactions are valid. Proof of Work has computers compete to solve hard puzzles, spending energy to earn the right to add a block — the model Bitcoin uses.

articles.title: Fake Wallet and Exchange Apps
articles.summary: Scammers publish counterfeit wallet and exchange apps, or send links to sideload them, hoping you will enter a seed phrase or log in with real credentials.

articles.title: What a Smart Contract Is
articles.summary: A smart contract is a program stored on a blockchain that runs exactly as written when its conditions are met, without a middleman to execute it.

articles.title: Bull Market vs Bear Market
articles.summary: A bull market is a sustained stretch of generally rising prices and optimism; a bear market is a prolonged period of falling prices and caution.

articles.title: Rug Pulls: What They Are and the Warning Signs
articles.summary: A rug pull is when the people behind a token drain its liquidity or dump their holdings, collapsing the price and leaving holders with something they cannot sell.

articles.title: What Staking Is
articles.summary: Staking means locking up coins to help secure a Proof-of-Stake network, and in return earning rewards paid by the protocol.

articles.title: Public Key, Private Key and Address
articles.summary: A private key is the secret that authorises spending from a wallet. A public key and the address derived from it are what you share to receive funds.

articles.title: Why Crypto Is So Volatile
articles.summary: Volatility measures how much and how quickly a price swings. Crypto is known for high volatility: double-digit daily moves are not unusual.

articles.title: What 24-Hour Trading Volume Tells You
articles.summary: Twenty-four-hour volume is the total value of an asset traded across markets in the past day. It is a measure of activity and interest, not of price direction.

articles.title: Bitcoin Dominance, Explained
articles.summary: Bitcoin dominance is Bitcoin's share of the entire crypto market's capitalisation. If the whole market is worth $2.5T and Bitcoin is $1.4T, dominance is about 56%.

articles.title: Circulating, Total and Max Supply — the Difference
articles.summary: Circulating supply is the number of coins available and in public hands right now. Total supply includes coins that exist but are locked, reserved or not yet released. Max supply is the hard ceiling a protocol will ever create, where one exists.
